editorial:
Imagine living a double life for years, keeping your true self hidden from the people you love most. That is exactly where you find Michael, a successful lawyer who has always played the part of the perfect son. He is gay, but his parents and grandmother have no idea. The vibe of this movie is heavy and emotional, but it feels very real. Everything changes when Michael gets a diagnosis of AIDS. Knowing his time is short, he can no longer keep his secrets. You get to see the raw tension as he brings his partner, Peter, home to meet a family that is completely unprepared for the news.

What really makes this work is the acting; you can feel the pain and the awkwardness in every scene. The pacing is slow, which helps you feel the weight of the sadness, though some parts might feel a bit like an old TV play. If you enjoy powerful dramas about family and forgiveness, you need to see this. Since it is an older film, you might not find it in 4K, but it is worth hunting down a digital rental on Apple TV or adding the DVD to your collection for a rainy day.
endingExplained: The movie ends with a bittersweet focus on family acceptance. After a lot of fighting and tears, Michael's parents eventually move past their shock and prejudice. They choose to love their son more than they hate his lifestyle. You see them coming together to support Michael and Peter during his final days. It does not have a happy cure, but it gives you a sense of peace knowing Michael died feeling seen and loved.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves powerful stories about family bonds and overcoming prejudice.
